## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Speech Technology for Conversational AI
  Code                    M2 · P2 (announced) — official code not published (course description not published)
  Team and workload       Instructor: master's team · \~24 h · building the complete voice loop — signal (Mel spectrogram/MFCC), ASR from GMM-HMM to CTC (loss derived), LAS, Whisper and streaming, TTS from the vocoder (WaveNet, HiFi-GAN) to diffusion/flow models, expressivity and cloning (ethics, audio watermarking), up to full-duplex conversational voices and speech LLMs — the bridge between Signal Processing (M1) and LLMs (M2).
  Status in the program   [M2]{.badge .m2}[Slot TBC · AI systems route]{.badge .position} · M2 program being finalized
  ----------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an NLP or signal-processing engineer who wants to master the full voice loop. **Empirical first**: the module starts from concrete failures — a word error rate of 4% in the studio that becomes 28% on a noisy phone line, a TTS system that clones a voice without any watermark — and only then names the tools (Mel features, CTC, Whisper, vocoders).

The course goes from recognition (ASR) to synthesis (TTS) to speech LLMs, and bridges Signal Processing (M1) and Large Language Models (M2).

### What you will be able to do

-   Choose and compute the representations of the speech signal (Mel spectrogram, MFCC) according to the use;
-   Explain the classical GMM-HMM pipeline and what caused its replacement;
-   Derive the CTC loss (sum over alignments, forward-backward) and implement it;
-   Compare LAS, Conformer and RNN-T according to the quality/latency trade-off, and explain Whisper's multi-task robustness;
-   Size a streaming system: chunking, voice activity detection, latency vs quality;
-   Explain the modern TTS chain: vocoders (WaveNet to HiFi-GAN), Tacotron 2, VITS, diffusion and flow approaches;
-   Control the expressivity of a synthesis (prosody, style tokens, SSML) and master the ethical issues of voice cloning;
-   Describe the complete conversational loop (VAD, turn-taking, full-duplex) and how multilingual speech LLMs work.

### Where this course fits in the program

An M2 module announced for period 2 (slot to be confirmed), on the site's AI systems route: it is the master's "multimodal" module devoted to the audio modality, designed as the joint production deployment of two prerequisites. **Prerequisites**: [Signal Processing](../m1p1-signal-processing/index.html) (windowing, Fourier transform, spectrograms — revisited in ch. 0) and [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html), whose multimodal chapter (ch. 8) announces the speech LLMs covered here at the end of the course.

**Downstream**: the module gives its voice component to the conversational assistant — the LLGA's application through-line, which crosses the agents of [Advanced Topics in Large Language Models](../m2-advanced-topics-llms/index.html) (ch. 9) and the production constraints of [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) (P99 latency, costs); it also extends the watermarking of the [Control in Generative AI](../m2-control-generative-ai/index.html) module to the audio side.

### Course outline

-   **Recap: the speech signal and its representations** — windowing, Mel spectrograms and MFCC: the raw material of the whole course.
-   **Classical ASR: the GMM-HMM pipeline** — the historical architecture, still useful to understand what neural methods replaced.
-   **CTC: the loss, derived** — learning without frame/phoneme alignment: the complete derivation of the loss that opened up deep ASR.
-   **Encoder-decoder: LAS, Conformer, RNN-T** — three architectural answers to the quality/latency trade-off.
-   **Whisper: robustness and multi-task** — what very large-scale supervised learning changes (and costs).
-   **Streaming: chunking, VAD, latency vs quality** — going from file to stream: split, detect speech, own the latency.
-   **Vocoders: from WaveNet to HiFi-GAN** — generating the waveform itself, and the path from slow autoregressive models to fast GANs.
-   **Neural TTS: Tacotron 2, VITS, diffusion and flow** — modern synthesis from text to spectrogram then to signal.
-   **Expressivity: prosody, style tokens, SSML** — not only saying, but *how* to say it.
-   **Voice conversion and cloning: ethics and watermarking** — the promises of cloning, its misuse, and how to mark generated audio.
-   **The conversational loop: VAD, turn-taking, full-duplex** — listening, waiting one's turn, interrupting oneself: real-time orchestration.
-   **Speech LLMs and multilingualism** — the speech signal fed directly into the language model: architectures and issues for low-resource languages.
-   **Exercises / Labs** — align a CTC, measure a WER, synthesize and watermark a voice clip.
-   **References** — the founding papers of neural ASR and TTS.

### How to study this module

-   Listen to every example audio of the course (originals, degraded, synthesized): the ear is here a measuring instrument to train as much as the WER.
-   Write the CTC forward-backward yourself on a mini-example by hand: it is the obligatory step to never again confuse alignment and decoding.
-   For each architecture, place it on the "latency/quality" axis and note what is computed online versus offline: it is the module's reading grid.
-   Wire up a mini "microphone → ASR → response → TTS → speaker" loop early, even a basic one, then improve it chapter after chapter.
-   Read ch. 9 (cloning, ethics) with the eye of a future professional: questions of consent and audio watermarking will arise in your projects from the internship onward.

::: note
[The LLGA perspective]{.tag} With speech LLMs, voice has become a first-class modality for language models: the LLGA master, which trains at the crossroads of LLMs and their applications, offers you here the complete chain — from spectrogram to speaking turn — rather than a simple overview. Conversational assistants (telephony, accessibility, embedded voice interfaces) are one of the most in-demand career paths in the field, and the module crosses all the master's skills: signal, LLMs, real-time streaming, ethics and control.
:::

## 0. Recap: the speech signal and its representations {#ch0}

Every model of this module reads or writes a spectrogram, so the course starts from the signal. This chapter recalls what the Signal Processing module established, then states the two problems of the module — recognition and synthesis — and how recognition is scored.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Prerequisites (Signal Processing M1 module) — what is assumed known
:::

-   **Sampling** (ch. 4): Shannon's theorem; speech is sampled at 16 kHz (ASR) or 24 kHz (synthesis), useful telephone band 300-3400 Hz, formants up to \~8 kHz;
-   **Time-frequency analysis** (ch. 6): STFT, Gabor windows, time-frequency trade-off — *the* spectrogram is the input of almost all the models in this module (cf. Signal Processing module ch. 6);
-   **Mel spectrogram and MFCC** (ch. 8): 25 ms frames every 10 ms, Hann window, Mel filter bank (perceptual scale linear below 1 kHz then logarithmic: $m = 2595\log_{10}(1 + f/700)$), 20-80 coefficients, possibly DCT (MFCC);
-   **Random signals** (ch. 7): power spectral density, periodogram — used by energy-based VADs (ch. 10) and spread-spectrum watermarking (ch. 9);
-   **Recurrent networks and transformers** ([Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch5) M1 ch. 5–6, or [Deep Learning P2](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-rnn) on its path, sections on recurrent networks and text generation): LSTM, attention $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})V$ — the ASR/TTS encoder is a transformer (ch. 3-4);
-   **Diffusion and VAE** ([Multimodal GenAI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html#ch3) M1 ch. 1 and 3, or [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch9) ch. 9 / [Deep Learning P2](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-generative) §7.3): ELBO, DDPM, noise prediction — the generative TTS models (ch. 7) descend directly from them; normalizing flows and flow matching are recalled in ch. 7.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — ASR and TTS, formalized]{.tag} **Recognition** (ASR): estimate the transcription $y$ (sequence of tokens — characters, phonemes, BPE) of an acoustic frame $x_{1:T}$ (Mel features, typically $T \approx 100$ frames per second of speech, one every 10 ms): model $p_\theta(y \mid x_{1:T})$.

**Synthesis** (TTS): the inverse, $p_\theta(x \mid y)$ — a *one-to-many* problem: a text can be said in infinitely many ways (voice, rate, emotion), which will structure all of ch. 7-8 (TTS is a *generation* problem, ASR a *decision* problem).

The reference ASR error is the **WER**:
$$\mathrm{WER} = \frac{S + D + I}{N},$$
substitutions/deletions/insertions obtained by word-level Levenshtein alignment between hypothesis and reference (lab 1).
:::

::: note
[The module's line — and why "conversational"]{.tag} The course follows the stack of a voice assistant: understand (ch. 1-5), speak (ch. 6-9), converse (ch. 10-11).

The technical thread: two *breaks* occurred —

1.  the abandonment of explicit alignment (HMM → CTC → attention → discrete tokens);
2.  the fusion of the three ASR+LLM+TTS building blocks into a single multimodal model (speech LLMs, ch. 11) that speaks and listens — where *full-duplex* conversation (ch. 10) becomes computable.

Speech regains its status there: the fastest (3-4 words/s produced, 5-8 understood) and most natural interface.
:::

::: note
[Module status]{.tag} Course proposed in the M2 brochure (period 2): the instructors are not yet confirmed; there is therefore no "research of the instructor" chapter — the content follows the standards of the field and constantly builds on the modules already covered (Signal Processing M1 for the signal, LLMs M2 for the language layer).
:::

## 1. Classical ASR: the GMM-HMM pipeline {#ch1}

A recognizer tuned on call-center audio collapses as soon as the accent or the microphone changes. To understand why, and what neural systems changed, this chapter presents the architecture that dominated speech recognition for thirty years: an acoustic model of sounds, a lexicon and a language model, combined by Bayesian decoding.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Three mistakes recur in this module: ignoring the acoustic domain (microphone, noise, accent) in which a system will be used, judging a recognizer by its WER alone, which ignores meaning, and deploying voice cloning without consent or watermarking (ch. 9).
:::

The historical pipeline (1980-2015) survives only as technical memories — but its formalism (emission model, chain of states, Bayesian decoding) reappears everywhere, up to the CTC forward-backward (ch. 2). We cover it in one structured chapter.

::: thm
[Theorem 1.1 — The GMM-HMM acoustic model and decoding]{.tag} One decomposes $p(x_{1:T} \mid w)$ with a hidden Markov chain over phonetic states $q_t$: each phoneme is a 3-state left-to-right HMM (beginning/middle/end), put in context (triphones); the emission of a state is a **Gaussian mixture** over the MFCCs (39 dimensions: 13 + first and second derivatives):
$$p(x_t \mid q_t = s) = \sum_{m=1}^{M_s} c_{sm}\, \mathcal N(x_t;\ \mu_{sm}, \Sigma_{sm}).$$

The retained transcription maximizes *Bayesian decoding*
$$\hat w = \arg\max_w\ p(x_{1:T} \mid w)\, p_{\mathrm{LM}}(w),$$
where $p_{\mathrm{LM}}$ is an n-gram language model (cf. NLP M1 module ch. 2).

The likelihood is computed by the *forward* recursion
$$\alpha_t(j) = \Big[\sum_i \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, a_{ij}\Big]\, b_j(x_t),$$
($\mathcal O(T N^2)$, $N$ states) and the best path by *Viterbi* (same recursion, max instead of the sum).

Training: EM (Baum-Welch) — cf. Machine Learning M1 module ch. 7 for the EM of latent-variable models.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Why GMM? And why is it dead?]{.tag}

1.  A Gaussian mixture is a universal density approximator (with enough components, any continuous density is approximated): it was the best parameterization *before* deep learning.
2.  Fatal flaws: MFCCs are not semantic features (the GMM models acoustic blocks, knows nothing about similar phones); the HMM assumes the signal locally stationary per state and conditional independence of the frames; above all, each piece (lexicon, contexts, LM) is optimized separately — impossible to align globally.

Neural systems *eat* raw data: 10,000 labeled hours replace 300 carefully curated ones (ch. 4).
:::

::: note
[What survives of the pipeline]{.tag} Three direct legacies:

1.  the acoustic + LM *fusion* at decoding (the "shallow fusion" reappears with LLMs to rescore N-bests);
2.  the *forward-backward* — the central algorithm of CTC in the next chapter;
3.  *forced alignment* (finding the instants of each word, still used for subtitling and training TTS).

Historical reference: Rabiner's tutorial (Proc. IEEE, 1989) remains a limpid read.
:::

## 2. CTC: the loss, derived {#ch2}

The central problem of neural ASR: the output (sequence of tokens $y$) is shorter than the input ($T$ frames) and *unaligned* — there is no label per frame. The solution of Graves et al. (ICML 2006): marginalize over *all* possible alignments. We derive everything: this is technical chapter no. 1 of the module.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Alignments and collapse]{.tag} The network emits at each frame a distribution $p_\theta(\cdot \mid x_{1:T}, t)$ over the extended alphabet $\mathcal V \cup \{\epsilon\}$ ($\epsilon$ = blank). A *path* $\pi \in (\mathcal V \cup \{\epsilon\})^T$ is a sequence of $T$ symbols, drawn independently:
$$p(\pi \mid x) = \prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(\pi_t \mid x, t).$$

The **collapse** map $\mathcal B$ first merges consecutive repetitions, then removes the blanks: $\mathcal B(\texttt{hheelllo}) = \texttt{helo}$ (each run of identical symbols counts once). Conversely, doubles *separated by a blank* survive:
$$\mathcal B(\texttt{l}\,\epsilon\,\texttt{l}) = \texttt{ll},$$
so that
$$\mathcal B(\texttt{hhe}\,\epsilon\,\texttt{l}\,\epsilon\,\texttt{lo}) = \texttt{hello}$$
— that is the whole art of CTC.

The CTC loss marginalizes:
$$p_\theta(y \mid x) \;=\; \sum_{\pi \in \mathcal B^{-1}(y)} p(\pi \mid x), \qquad \mathcal L_{\mathrm{CTC}} = -\log p_\theta(y \mid x).$$

*Why the blank is indispensable*: without it, a collapsed $\texttt{ll}$ could not be distinguished from $\texttt{l}$ — impossible to write "bonne" with a double n. The blank carries the boundary information.
:::

::: key
[Key result — the CTC loss]{.tag}
$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CTC}} = -\log \sum_{\pi \in \mathcal B^{-1}(y)} \prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(\pi_t \mid x, t)$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.2 — Counting by hand (T = 4, y = "ab")]{.tag} Extended sequence $\ell = (\epsilon, a, \epsilon, b, \epsilon)$: the label with a blank before, between and after the letters (length $S = 2|y| + 1 = 5$).

A path of length 4 collapses to $\texttt{ab}$ exactly when it reads "blanks, a run of $a$, blanks, a run of $b$, blanks", each run of blanks possibly empty (writing $\texttt{-}$ for $\epsilon$).

Since the runs of $a$ and $b$ take at least one frame each, the two remaining frames are distributed among five runs:
$$\binom{6}{2} = 15 \text{ paths:}$$

-   two blanks: $\texttt{--ab}$, $\texttt{-a-b}$, $\texttt{-ab-}$, $\texttt{a--b}$, $\texttt{a-b-}$, $\texttt{ab--}$;
-   one blank: $\texttt{-aab}$, $\texttt{-abb}$, $\texttt{aa-b}$, $\texttt{aab-}$, $\texttt{a-bb}$, $\texttt{abb-}$;
-   none: $\texttt{aaab}$, $\texttt{aabb}$, $\texttt{abbb}$.

A path such as $\texttt{a-ab}$ is *not* valid: the blank separates the two $a$'s, which then both survive ($\mathcal B = \texttt{aab}$).

Each path contributes its product of 4 probabilities: $p(y \mid x)$ is the sum of the 15; exercise 3 computes it for numerical values, exercise 4 checks with the implementation.

The number of paths grows exponentially (up to $(|\mathcal V| + 1)^T$): direct summation is impossible — hence the forward-backward.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — CTC forward-backward (recursions and gradient, proven)]{.tag} Let $p_t(k) = p_\theta(k \mid x, t)$, and $\ell$ the extended sequence. The *forward variables* $\alpha_t(s) = p(\ell_{1:s} \text{ reached at frame } t)$ follow
$$\alpha_t(s) = \Big[\alpha_{t-1}(s) + \alpha_{t-1}(s{-}1) + \mathbf 1\{\ell_s \neq \epsilon,\ \ell_s \neq \ell_{s-2}\}\, \alpha_{t-1}(s{-}2)\Big]\cdot p_t(\ell_s),$$
initialized $\alpha_1(1) = p_1(\epsilon)$, $\alpha_1(2) = p_1(\ell_2)$, the rest at 0 (one cannot "jump" ahead). Symmetrically $\beta_t(s)$ (backward, from the end).

Then
$$p(y \mid x) = \alpha_T(S) + \alpha_T(S{-}1), \qquad \alpha_t(s)\,\beta_t(s) = p\big(y \mid x,\ \pi_t = \ell_s\big)\cdot p_t(\ell_s),$$
and the gradient of the loss is written in closed form
$$\frac{\partial \mathcal L_{\mathrm{CTC}}}{\partial p_t(k)} = -\,\frac{1}{p(y \mid x)}\ \frac{1}{p_t(k)} \sum_{s\,:\,\ell_s = k} \alpha_t(s)\, \beta_t(s).$$

::: proof
**Step 1 (decomposition by the state at $t$).** The sum over paths partitions according to the position $s$ occupied at frame $t$. Each path passing through $\ell_s$ at $t$ factorizes into three factors:
$$\text{(prefix reaching } \ell_s \text{ at } t) \times p_t(\ell_s) \times (\text{suffix from } \ell_s \text{ at } t{+}1)$$
— hence
$$\alpha_t(s)\beta_t(s) = p(y, \pi_t = \ell_s \mid x)$$
(careful: the definition of $\beta$ includes the $p_t$ factor or not depending on the convention; with the one above, $\alpha_t(s)$ contains $p_t(\ell_s)$ and $\beta_t(s)$ does not).

**Step 2 (recursion).** For the path to be at $\ell_s$ at $t$, it was at $s$, $s{-}1$ or $s{-}2$ at $t{-}1$.

The jump of two positions is forbidden *except* if $\ell_s$ is a real letter different from $\ell_{s-2}$ (otherwise two identical letters would be merged by the collapse; and one never jumps *over* a letter).

**Step 3 (gradient).** $p(y \mid x) = \sum_{\pi} \prod_{t'} p_{t'}(\pi_{t'})$; each term using $p_t(k)$ corresponds to the paths with $\pi_t = k \in \ell$, whose total sum equals $\sum_{s:\ell_s = k}\alpha_t(s)\beta_t(s)$. Differentiating the log:
$$\partial \mathcal L/\partial p_t(k) = -\partial p(y \mid x)/\partial p_t(k) \cdot 1/p(y \mid x),$$
and
$$\partial p(y \mid x)/\partial p_t(k) = \big[\sum_s \alpha\beta\big] / p_t(k)$$
(each path where $\pi_t = k$ is linear in $p_t(k)$).

**Complexity**: $\mathcal O(T \cdot S)$ — two tables of $T \times (2|y|+1)$, versus the exponential enumeration. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — CTC inference and model assumptions]{.tag}

1.  *Greedy decoding*: $\hat y = \mathcal B(\arg\max_k p_t(k)\ \text{for each } t)$ — fast, suboptimal; *beam search*: maintain $K$ prefixes with their truncated $\alpha$ scores, merge equal prefixes after collapse, optionally rescored by an LM.
2.  *Assumptions of CTC*: conditional independence of the frames (no internal language model — hence the external LM) and *monotone* distribution (the alignment goes left to right): perfect for reading, forbidden for translation (ch. 3 to break free of it).
:::

::: note
[CTC's posterity]{.tag} CTC lives everywhere in 2026: forced alignment (ch. 1), the pre-training of wav2vec 2 (CTC objective), and — above all — **RNN-T** (ch. 3) is a CTC extended to real time, with a blank reinterpreted as "move forward in time".

By contrast, Whisper is *not* CTC (attention encoder-decoder, ch. 4): knowing how to say "this one marginalizes alignments, that one generates them" is a classic oral-exam question.
:::

## 3. Encoder-decoder: LAS, Conformer, RNN-T {#ch3}

CTC assumes that the frames are conditionally independent and has no language model of its own. This chapter presents the three architectures that lift these limits in different ways — by learning the alignment with attention (LAS), by improving the encoder (Conformer), or by adding a prediction network while keeping streaming possible (RNN-T).

::: thm
[Theorem 3.1 — LAS: Listen, Attend and Spell (Chan et al., ICASSP 2016)]{.tag} **Listen**: a pyramidal BLSTM (then transformer) encoder compacts the frames $x_{1:T}$ into states $h_j$.

**Attend**: at each output step $i$, an additive attention computes
$$e_{ij} = v^\top \tanh\big(W_s s_{i-1} + W_h h_j\big), \qquad \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp e_{ij}}{\sum_{j'} \exp e_{ij'}}, \qquad c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij}\, h_j,$$
(*location-sensitive* attention in practice: the past weights $a_{i-1}$ enter $e_{ij}$ to make it monotone and avoid skipped/repeated words).

**Spell**: an autoregressive decoder emits $y_i$ from $(s_{i-1}, y_{i-1}, c_i)$, trained by teacher forcing and cross-entropy.

The loss is no longer a marginalization: the attention *learns* the alignment — and can reorder it (used for speech translation).

Two inherited weaknesses: *exposure bias* (trained on the reference, tested on its own errors) and the impossibility of strict streaming (all of $x$ is read before the first token).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Conformer: local convolution + global attention (Gulati et al., Interspeech 2020)]{.tag} The Conformer block chains ("macaron" style) two feed-forward networks with a 1/2 factor around

1.  a multi-head attention with *relative* positional encoding (captures long context — sentences span hundreds of frames), and
2.  a deep convolutional module (pointwise convolution $\to$ depthwise with dilation, GLU/SiLU, LayerNorm) that captures local phonetics (formants, transitions).

The takeaway intuition: attention alone is bad at the fine local patterns of speech, convolution alone does not see the context — the sandwich of the two dominated industrial ASR 2021-2024 (before being absorbed by the foundation models of ch. 4: wav2vec 2, HuBERT, Whisper encoder).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — RNN-T (Graves, 2012): the CTC that speaks in real time]{.tag} The RNN-transducer combines an *encoder* $f_t$ (frame $\to$ state, causal — processed on the fly) and a *prediction network* $g_u$ (tokens already emitted $\to$ state); a joint network produces
$$P(k \mid t, u) = \mathrm{softmax}\big(W\, f_t + W'\, g_u + b\big)_{k}, \qquad k \in \mathcal V \cup \{\epsilon\},$$
and the likelihood sums over all paths of the $(t, u)$ grid — it is the forward-backward of Theorem 2.3, transposed onto a $T \times U$ trellis where $\epsilon$ = "advance in $t$ without emitting".

Decisive property: the encoder is *causal*, each $f_t$ is computable as soon as the frame arrives — RNN-T is the queen architecture of **streaming** ASR (ch. 5), notably on device.

Cost: an $\mathcal O(TU)$ lattice at training and the CTC monotonicity assumption (no reordering).
:::

  Architecture      Alignment                Loss                       Streaming           Internal LM?               Typical use
  ----------------- ------------------------ -------------------------- ------------------- -------------------------- --------------------------------
  GMM-HMM (ch. 1)   explicit states          EM (Baum-Welch)            yes                 no (n-gram)                legacy, old telephony
  CTC (ch. 2)       marginalized, monotone   forward-backward           partial             no                         forced alignment, pre-training
  LAS (ch. 3)       learned (attention)      cross-entropy              no                  yes (AR decoder)           offline, max quality
  RNN-T (ch. 3)     monotone trellis         2D forward-backward        yes                 partial (prediction net)   assistants, mobile
  Whisper (ch. 4)   generated (attention)    multi-task cross-entropy   no (30 s windows)   yes                        general transcription

## 4. Whisper: robustness and multi-task {#ch4}

The architectures of chapter 3 were trained on a few thousand carefully transcribed hours and broke on real-world audio. This chapter shows how Whisper obtained robustness from a plain encoder-decoder trained on a very large amount of imperfectly labelled web audio.

::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Whisper (Radford et al., ICML 2023): the strength of the weak]{.tag} Trained on $\approx$ 680,000 hours of *weakly supervised* audio/text pairs collected from the web (versus a few hundred to thousand carefully curated hours before), Whisper is a simple transformer encoder-decoder (39M-1.5B parameters); the audio is cut into 30 s windows, log-Mel 80 bins.

The output is a *sequence of special tokens + text*: `<|startoftranscript|>` $\to$ language $\to$ task (transcribe/translate into English) $\to$ timestamps $\to$ text — everything (language identifier, translation decision, time) is *learned as language*, no dedicated module.

Results: unprecedented robustness to noise/reverberation/accents (trained on real, not read data), WER close to humans on clean English; best zero-shot performance on most languages at the time.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Why it works: the scaling law of dirty data]{.tag}

1.  *Coverage*: robustness is not a module, it is a consequence of diversity — the 680 kh cover real-world mess (background noise, music, accents), whereas LibriSpeech (1000 h of read books) overlearns clean reading;
2.  *Filtering beats labeling*: the training pipeline filters aggressively (language detection, audio-text matching by an initial ASR, anti-hallucination heuristics) rather than correcting by hand — the *moderately clean but massive* data wins;
3.  *Multi-task as regularization*: transcribing AND translating AND timestamping share one encoder — translation forces semantic, not only acoustic, representations.

Documented limits: hallucinations on long silences (looped repetitions — the model "invents" text), no native streaming (ch. 5), difficult fine specialization.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — French in the crosshairs]{.tag} On clean English, a good system reaches human WER (\~5%); the same model on spontaneous contemporary French typically does 2 to 3 times worse (accents, speaking rates, code-switching, proper names) — lab 1 measures it.

Three French phenomena to know for engineering:

-   *liaison* (*les amis* is pronounced [le.za.mi]: the *s* of *les* is heard at the start of the next word — spelling is not phonetics, and the ASR must recover the written form);
-   *enchaînement* (final consonant tied to the next vowel: word boundaries blur in the spectrogram);
-   *number verbalization* (1996: "mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-seize" or "dix-neuf cent quatre-vingt-seize"? — normalization ambiguity, both are valid; cf. ch. 8 for the reverse direction in TTS).
:::

## 5. Streaming: chunking, VAD, latency vs quality {#ch5}

Conversing means answering fast: the ASR must produce words *while* one speaks. This chapter deals with the "offline $\to$ streaming" transformation, whose cost is measured in WER added per second gained.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Latencies of a streaming ASR]{.tag} The **algorithmic latency** of a chunked encoder (*chunking*) of size $L$ frames with a lookahead of $R$ frames equals
$$\lambda = (L + R)\,\Delta, \qquad \Delta = \text{frame step } (10\ \mathrm{ms}),$$
— one cannot predict before having heard the context.

The **real-time factor** (RTF) measures the computational cost: computation time / audio duration (RTF $<$ 1 required, $\ll 1$ on device). The **first-word latency** adds the VAD and the endpointing decision (ch. 10).

A conversational voice assistant targets $\lambda \leq 300$ ms end to end (exercise 5) — humans answer in \~200 ms (ch. 10): this is *the* structuring constraint of the field.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Three streaming architectures (Moritz et al., ICASSP 2020, for the first)]{.tag}

1.  **Block attention**: the transformer encoder processes windows of $L$ frames with a complete left context (memory) and a bounded right lookahead $R$ — the attention is *masked* beyond; the larger $R$ grows, the more the WER drops and the latency rises (curve of Proposition 5.3);
2.  **Causal RNN-T** (Theorem 3.3): pure encoder $L = 1$, $R = 0$ — emission from the frame on; the lookahead is reinjected into the *prediction* network (the right context comes from the tokens already emitted); standard on mobile;
3.  **Asynchronous re-scoring**: a first streaming pass gives the real-time display, an offline model (Whisper) *re-corrects* the final transcription with a few hundred ms of delay — the interface shows the text "correcting itself" (the design of 2026 assistants: the truth arrives one second later, reactivity is immediate).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — The latency/quality curve, and how to read it]{.tag} For each point $(L, R)$ (or each model choice): measure WER and first-word latency on a *fixed* test corpus; plot WER($\lambda$).

Typical shape: the WER is high at very small latency, drops quickly as $\lambda$ grows to about 200-300 ms (the useful context of a phoneme and of its transitions fits in about 200 ms), then reaches a plateau where extra context no longer helps.

Engineer's reading: choose the elbow point; scientific reading: the curve *is* a control curve (fidelity against resource) — exactly the grid of the Control in Generative AI module (M2, ch. 2 and 9), where "diversity" is replaced by "reactivity".
:::

::: note
[VAD: the gateway of the stream]{.tag} *Voice activity detection* decides, window by window (10-30 ms), whether the frame contains speech: energy + periodicity (historical), energy/noise GMM (Signal module ch. 7), lightweight networks (Silero VAD — the lab's tool).

Two errors of opposite cost: the *false alarm* sends noise to the ASR (Whisper hallucinations on silences!); the *miss* cuts word beginnings (the initial French "euh").

The VAD also initiates *endpointing* — deciding that the user has finished speaking (ch. 10): even more sensitive, because it sets the *perceived* latency of the whole system.
:::

## 6. Vocoders: from WaveNet to HiFi-GAN {#ch6}

Synthesis ends with a waveform: tens of thousands of samples per second, whose phase is not contained in the spectrogram. This chapter presents the vocoders that generate it, from the slow but faithful WaveNet to the fast HiFi-GAN used in production.

::: thm
[Theorem 6.1 — WaveNet (van den Oord et al., 2016): autoregression over the samples]{.tag} The vocoder models the waveform directly:
$$p(x) = \prod_{t=1}^{T_{\mathrm{s}}} p(x_t \mid x_{<t},\, c),$$
with $T_{\mathrm{s}}$ the number of samples (24,000 per second of audio), $x_t$ $\mu$-law quantized over 256 levels, $c$ the conditioning (Mel, speaker).

Architecture: **dilated causal convolutions** — layer $k$ looks $2^k$ samples back (dilations 1, 2, 4, ..., 512, stacked): the receptive field grows *exponentially* with depth ($\approx 2^L$ for $L$ layers), where a non-dilated convolution would require $2^L$ layers.

Quality: close to human speech in subjective tests (MOS above 4, versus \~4.5 for the ground truth).

Fatal flaw: generating one second of speech takes 24,000 sequential steps — orders of magnitude slower than real time, unusable in production.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — HiFi-GAN (Kong et al., NeurIPS 2020): speed through the adversary]{.tag} Complete reversal: the generator is *parallel feed-forward* (upsampling by transposed convolutions from the 80-bin Mel to the waveform, then multi-receptive-field dilated convolutions for phase coherence).

Training is *adversarial* (GAN recap: Multimodal GenAI M1 module ch. 2) with two families of discriminators — *multi-period* (they rearrange the waveform into matrices of periods 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 to trap periodic artifacts: the "buzz") and *multi-scale* — plus an L1 loss on the reconstructed Mel to anchor the content.

Result: WaveNet quality, parallel generation — orders of magnitude faster than real time on GPU, the industry's default vocoder.

To remember from the chapter: the opposition between *sequential generation* (autoregressive over 24,000 samples per second) and *parallel architecture + perceptual losses* dictates all of modern TTS.
:::

::: note
[The Mel as a contractual interface]{.tag} The two stages of the TTS (ch. 7) communicate via the Mel spectrogram: 80 bins, one frame roughly every 12 ms (\~ 80 Hz), logarithmic scale — the vocoder's *specification sheet*.

Changing the definition (sampling frequency, hop, n_bins) breaks the model/vocoder compatibility — the first experiment of lab 2. And the Mel is not invertible (phase lost): the whole difficulty of the vocoder is to *re-invent* a coherent phase — hence the period discriminators.
:::

## 7. Neural TTS: Tacotron 2, VITS, diffusion and flow {#ch7}

Given a vocoder, it remains to turn text into a spectrogram — a one-to-many problem, since a sentence can be said in many ways. This chapter follows the three generations of answers: an attention model that writes the Mel frame by frame, an end-to-end stochastic model, and iterative diffusion and flow models.

::: thm
[Theorem 7.1 — Tacotron 2 (Shen et al., ICASSP 2018): the two-stage scheme]{.tag} Stage 1: an *attentional* encoder-decoder reads the text (graphemes) and writes the Mel frame by frame — the *location-sensitive* attention learns the text→acoustic alignment there (same mechanism as LAS in ch. 3, applied in reverse); training by teacher forcing on the reference Mels.

Stage 2: a WaveNet (ch. 6) turns the Mel into a wave. Historical quality: natural on read sentences.

Two chronic diseases: *attention failure* (skipped or stuttered words on long or out-of-distribution sentences) and *excessive determinism* — one text, a single voice/rate (the one-to-many of Definition 0.1 denied by training toward the *average* Mel: smoothed, metallic output).
:::

::: recap
[Recap — flows and flow matching]{.tag} *Change of variables* ([Refresher Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html#ch2) Theorem 2.4). If $z$ has density $p_Z$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $x = f(z)$ for a differentiable bijection $f$, then
$$
\log p_X(x) = \log p_Z\big(f^{-1}(x)\big) + \log \big|\det J_{f^{-1}}(x)\big| .
$$
The Jacobian term corrects for the local stretching of volume, so that the density of $x$ still integrates to 1.

*Normalizing flow.* One composes simple bijections whose log-determinants are cheap. In an affine *coupling* layer, half of the coordinates pass unchanged and the other half are rescaled and shifted by functions $s$ and $t$ of the first half:
$$
y_{1:k} = z_{1:k}, \qquad y_{k+1:d} = z_{k+1:d} \odot e^{s(z_{1:k})} + t(z_{1:k}), \qquad \log\big|\det J_f\big| = \sum_j s_j(z_{1:k}).
$$
The Jacobian is triangular, so the exact log-likelihood costs one pass (the log-determinant enters it with a minus sign), and a flow used alone is trained by maximizing it. VITS stacks such layers in their shift-only form ($s = 0$, log-determinant zero) to make its text-conditioned prior more flexible; the whole model is still trained on an ELBO.

*Flow matching* (Lipman et al., ICLR 2023) learns instead a velocity field $v_\theta(x, t)$, for $t \in [0, 1]$, whose differential equation carries Gaussian noise $x_0$ at $t = 0$ to data $x_1$ at $t = 1$. Along the straight path from a noise sample to a data sample the velocity is constant, which gives the *conditional flow-matching loss*:
$$
x_t = (1 - t)\, x_0 + t\, x_1, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, x_1}\, \big\| v_\theta(x_t, t) - (x_1 - x_0) \big\|^2 .
$$
Its minimizer is the conditional mean of $x_1 - x_0$ given $x_t$: the velocity field that transports the whole noise distribution onto the data distribution. Training never simulates the equation; sampling integrates it with an ODE solver in a few to a few dozen steps. Voicebox (theorem 7.3) conditions $v_\theta$ on the text and on the unmasked part of the Mel.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — VITS (Kim et al., ICML 2021): one-stage, stochastic, end-to-end]{.tag} Three ideas that answer Tacotron's diseases.

1.  *VAE:* a variational encoder encodes the target speech into $z$; the decoder (HiFi-GAN) writes the wave from $z$ — the *noise* of the prior explores the multiplicity of ways of saying;
2.  *normalizing flow:* a flow (exact change of variables, recalled in the box above) aligns the distribution of the text-conditioned latent with the prior, which makes training end-to-end (an ELBO whose prior density is exact, plus an adversary);
3.  *implicit monotone alignment* (MAS: search for the optimal monotone alignment between text and Mel, refined at each step).

Result: a single text→wave network, parallel, stochastic — the first "industrializable" generation of TTS (YourTTS, ch. 9, derives from it).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 7.3 — Iterative generation arrives: Grad-TTS then Voicebox]{.tag}

**Grad-TTS (Popov et al., ICML 2021)**: an encoder predicts, for each phone, the *target mean* $\mu(x)$ of a Gaussian in Mel space; a *diffusion* decoder (DDPM — cf. Multimodal GenAI M1 module ch. 3) turns a noise $\mathcal N(0, I)$ into a Mel around $\mu$, guided by the noise prediction $\hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \mu)$; a duration predictor handles the number of frames per phone.

Quality grows with the number of steps... like latency: the step/quality curve is *the* trade-off curve of the Control module (M2) ch. 9, in TTS version.

**Voicebox (Le et al., 2023)**: *conditional flow matching in infilling mode* — one masks a region of the Mel and regenerates *only it*, the context remaining fixed: the same machinery as the inpainting of the graph diffusion DiGress ([Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch9) 9.5) transported into acoustics; its loss is the conditional flow-matching loss of the box above, with the text and the unmasked frames as conditions.

Immediate applications: editing a word in a sentence while keeping the voice, de-noising, voice translation... and zero-shot cloning from a few seconds of reference.

Non-autoregressive and parallel: the dominant family of research TTS 2024-2026.
:::

  System                 Paradigm                    Alignment             Stochastic?           Streaming          Native cloning
  ---------------------- --------------------------- --------------------- --------------------- ------------------ ----------------------------
  Tacotron 2 + WaveNet   AR attention + AR vocoder   learned attention     no                    no                 no
  VITS                   VAE + flow + GAN            implicit MAS          yes (prior)           difficult          via speaker emb. (YourTTS)
  Grad-TTS               diffusion to Mel            predicted durations   yes (initial noise)   per step           no
  Voicebox               flow matching, infilling    none (conditioned)    yes                   region by region   yes (3 s prompt)

::: ex
[Example 7.4 — Latency budget of a conversational TTS]{.tag} Goal: < 300 ms between the end of the LLM's decision and the first sound.

-   An AR Tacotron-like: the first *sentence* must be synthesized before the first sound (if one wants the intonation) — 1-2 s of lead time required: prohibitive.
-   VITS: the first *chunk* of Mel (a few frames) suffices — \~100 ms.
-   Voicebox: one must bound the number of sampling steps: 4-10 steps (instead of 50-100) with distillation, otherwise quality drops (the curve of thm. 7.3).

Conclusion: the full-duplex of ch. 10 was only possible after the non-autoregressive revolution — architecture and conversation are coupled constraints.
:::

## 8. Expressivity: prosody, style tokens, SSML {#ch8}

A synthesis can be intelligible and still sound flat or say a sentence with the wrong intention. This chapter describes what expressivity is made of and the two ways of controlling it: soft control through learned style latents, hard control through markup.

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — Prosody, three continuous sliders]{.tag} The manner of saying decomposes into $F_0$ (melody, in Hz — \~100-200 Hz for men, 160-300 for women, final fall of declarative utterances), *duration* (contrastive lengthening: a stretched "énorme"), *energy* (accents, stressed words).

These sliders are *continuous and intertwined*: the TTS must predict them all, and text alone is ambiguous (one neutral sentence, ten valid readings) — it is the one-to-many of ch. 7, aesthetic version.

French adds its signature: *final* group accent (not lexical as in English), interrogative rise without inversion, sustained rate that makes segmentation critical.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 8.2 — Global Style Tokens (Wang et al., Interspeech 2018): style as a controllable latent]{.tag} A *reference encoder* reads a reference audio (a few seconds) and produces an embedding; an attention reads this embedding over a *bank of style tokens* (small learned dictionary of "manners of saying"); the weighted vector conditions the Tacotron (rendezvous of ch. 7).

Three uses:

-   *transfer* (give the audio of an enthusiastic speaker, generate the target text with their prosody);
-   *control* (move the embedding in token space — attenuate "aggressive");
-   *exploration* (the tokens spontaneously organize into interpretable axes: rate, energy, emotion).

It is the steering vector of the Control module (M2) ch. 4, applied to TTS: a latent direction read from contrasts, added instead of learned — same virtues (soft, composable control), same limits (no guarantee).
:::

::: def
[Definition 8.3 — SSML: the hard control of production]{.tag} The *Speech Synthesis Markup Language* (W3C) is the control language of industrial TTS: pauses (`<break time="500ms"/>`), rate/pitch (`<prosody rate="+10%" pitch="+2st">`), emphasis (`<emphasis>`), pronunciation (`<phoneme alphabet="ipa" ph="ʁə.ʒan">`), dates and numbers.

It is a **hard constraint** in the sense of the Control module ch. 2: the engine is *obliged* to obey (exact pause), as opposed to the soft conditioning of style tokens.

**Text normalization** (front-end): "1 234 567 €" $\to$ "un million deux cent trente-quatre mille cinq cent soixante-sept euros" is the hidden half of TTS — neural systems integrate the front-end (letter tokenizer) at the price of amusing errors (acronyms, "SARS-CoV-2": to be tested in lab 2).
:::

::: note
[Controlling what, and how: the complete grid]{.tag} Chapter recap in the taxonomy of the Control module (M2):

  Target         Soft mechanism                          Hard mechanism
  -------------- --------------------------------------- -------------------------------
  Voice          speaker embedding (ch. 9)               per-speaker model (fine-tune)
  Prosody        style tokens, audio prompt (Voicebox)   SSML prosody/phoneme
  Segmentation   duration predictor                      SSML break, max length
  Content        LLM upstream (referral to LLMs M2)      pronunciation lexicon

In production: the two columns coexist — SSML for precision (announcements, accessibility), latents for naturalness (conversation).
:::

## 9. Voice conversion and cloning: ethics and watermarking {#ch9}

The same models that give an assistant a pleasant voice can give anyone's voice to a fraudster from a few seconds of recording. This chapter explains how conversion and cloning work, what the law and the engineer must do about them, and how generated audio is watermarked.

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Conversion, adaptation, zero-shot cloning]{.tag} *Voice conversion*: re-emit *what* a source voice says *with the timbre* of a target voice (content preserved, speaker changed).

*Zero-shot cloning*: synthesize *any text* in a given voice from an *audio prompt* of a few seconds (VALL-E, Voicebox: conditioning by reference, ch. 7).

Technically: a speaker embedding (learned by speaker verification — the GE2E loss of Wan et al., 2018, aligns the embeddings of the same voice); YourTTS (ICML 2022) adds it to VITS (the TTS of ch. 7 becomes multi-speaker in one training).

VALL-E (Microsoft, 2023) treats cloning as language: AR over the EnCodec *acoustic tokens* (ch. 11), the 3 s prompt serving as prefix — TTS is absorbed by the LLM paradigm.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 9.2 — Ethics: the law follows (slowly), the engineer decides (fast)]{.tag} Cloning from 3 s of reference makes possible: voice fraud (calls to the "boss"), audio disinformation, impersonation.

Frameworks: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act, art. 50) imposes *transparency* — systems generating or manipulating image/voice must mark their outputs machine-readably; in France, the voice is protected as an attribute of personality (civil case law on imitation).

For the engineer, the operational answer is technical: *consent* (voice datasets under a clear license — lab 2 uses only authorized voices), *marking* (watermarking, below), *detection* (provenance: cf. Explainability module ch. 9 for text, the logic is identical).

The exam question: "why is TTS watermarking *easier* than text watermarking?" — because the output space is continuous and the channel capacity is immense (ch. 6): one can hide bits without perceptible loss... but the channel degrades under compressions.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 9.3 — Audio watermarking: from spread spectrum to networks]{.tag}

*Classical*: spread-spectrum watermarking — add a low-energy pseudo-random noise (key $k$), masked by the psychoacoustic threshold effect, in a time-frequency domain (STFT — Signal Processing M1 modules ch. 6-7: time-frequency analysis and random signals are proven there); detection by correlation with the key — the *exact* structure of the textual green/red watermark (ch. 6 of the Control module): a pseudo-random key, a hypothesis test, a strength/quality trade-off.

*Neural*: **WavMark** (2023) hides \~32 bits per second of speech with a learned encoder/detector, robust to re-encodings.

**AudioSeal** (Meta, ICASSP 2024) adds *localization*: a sample-level detector indicates *which* segments are synthetic (adversarial generator/detector, perceptual loss).

Marking *during* generation (in-generation) applies the watermark in the TTS itself — inseparable from the output.

Evaluation protocol: ROC curves detection rate / false positives, under attack (mp3, re-voicing, reverberation) — the robustness budget of the Control module ch. 10, word for word.
:::

::: ex
[Example 9.4 — Voice fraud in 3 steps (and its 3 countermeasures)]{.tag}

1.  3 s of public voice $\to$ zero-shot cloning;
2.  urgency script generated by an LLM (referral to LLMs M2);
3.  vishing call.

Countermeasures:

-   *channel*: automatic call-back on a known number (the most robust control is organizational);
-   *challenge* posed by the interlocutor (off-script question — conversational TTS answer these better and better, cf. ch. 10);
-   *provenance*: watermark verified at reception if both phones support it.

Moral of the module: no single layer suffices — defense in depth.
:::

## 10. The conversational loop: VAD, turn-taking, full-duplex {#ch10}

Recognition and synthesis are not yet a conversation: the system must also know when the user has finished, answer within a human delay, and cope with interruptions. This chapter measures the human speaking turn and shows how systems went from a pipeline with thresholds to full-duplex models.

::: thm
[Theorem 10.1 — The human speaking turn, in numbers]{.tag} Human conversation alternates turns with a median delay on the order of 200 ms — measured across a dozen languages (Stivers et al., PNAS 2009); yet planning and pronouncing the first word of a turn takes \~600 ms: humans *anticipate* the end of the other's turn (prosodic, syntactic, pragmatic cues) to prepare their own.

An assistant that listens to everything, waits for silence, transcribes, thinks, synthesizes, shows \~1.5-3 s of latency — *five to ten times too slow*: turn-taking is the real conversational bottleneck, not intelligence.

Reference framework: the survey by Skantze (Computer Speech & Language, 2021): transition-relevance points (TRP), end-of-turn prediction (end-of-turn: classifier on a sliding window — VAD + prosody + syntax), *backchannels* ("hmm", audible nods: listening without taking the turn).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 10.2 — Pipeline: endpointing as control]{.tag} Deciding "the user is done" is an error/latency trade-off: cutting too early = interruptions (the assistant speaks *over* — the most badly perceived error), cutting too late = dead silences.

Parameters: silence threshold $\tau_s$ (typically 300-700 ms), depth of context (rising prosody? incomplete syntax?), and *policy* (letting long hesitations speak).

Formalization: a sequential test — detect the "end of turn" regime change as early as possible under a false-positive constraint; the same fidelity/cost curve as streaming ASR (ch. 5), this time at the *dialogue* level.

Modern implementation: the end-of-turn predictor becomes a small *multi-modal* model (audio + partial text) that replaces hand-tuned thresholds.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 10.3 — Full-duplex: dGSLM then Moshi (the 2023-2024 leap)]{.tag}

**dGSLM** (Nguyen et al., TACL 2023): the first *entirely vocal* dialogue model — two streams of HuBERT tokens (discretized speech, ch. 11) run in parallel; the model learns *by itself* alternation and overlaps (simultaneous laughs): proof of concept that turn-taking is *learnable* without text.

**Moshi** (Défossez et al., Kyutai, 2024): the first real-time full-duplex voice assistant. Three pieces:

1.  the neural codec *Mimi* (descendant of EnCodec, ch. 11) tokenizes audio at low rate (\~12.5 frames/s) into two streams: semantic and acoustic;
2.  the *multi-stream* architecture: the tokens of *Moshi* (the model's voice) and of the *user* are predicted *in parallel*, not in alternation — the model can cut itself off or fall silent during an interruption;
3.  the *inner monologue*: each audio token of the model is aligned with its corresponding *text* token — the text guides, the audio realizes; theoretical latency \~200 ms (the human target of thm. 10.1), dialogue memory via the transformer context.

The module's loop is closed: VAD, endpointing, ASR-LLM-TTS pipeline *disappear* into a single generative model — the next topic.
:::

::: note
[What full-duplex changes in practice]{.tag}

1.  *Interruptions*: handled natively (the user stream continues to be predicted while Moshi speaks — the model "hears itself" speak);
2.  *Backchannels*: emergent, unscripted;
3.  *The voice of machines*: unique and marked vocal identity (AI Act transparency obligations, ch. 9);
4.  *the risk*: human latency makes the machine socially *indistinguishable* — watermarking (ch. 9) becomes the only frontier.

To be debated in session: should a 200 ms assistant announce itself?
:::

## 11. Speech LLMs and multilingualism {#ch11}

The last step removes the boundary between speech and text models: if audio can be cut into discrete tokens, a language model can read and write it directly. This chapter shows how audio is tokenized, the three ways of grafting audio onto an LLM, and what this changes for the thousands of languages with little data.

::: def
[Definition 11.1 — Tokenizing audio: neural codecs and RVQ]{.tag} A neural *codec* (EnCodec: Défossez et al., 2022) compresses speech with a convolutional auto-encoder constrained by a **residual vector quantization** (RVQ): the continuous latent is approximated by a sum of vectors from successive codebooks — each frame (at 24 kHz: one frame $\approx$ 320 samples, \~75 Hz) becomes a stack of \~2-32 discrete indices.

Result: speech becomes a *text* of tokens — consumable by a transformer.

The hierarchy of **AudioLM** (Borsos et al., 2023) orders these tokens: first *semantic* (discretized units of a self-supervised model — wav2vec 2/HuBERT — that capture the content), then *coarse* then *fine acoustic* (timbre, environment): generating in this order guarantees the content before the texture. It is the architecture of dGSLM and Moshi (ch. 10).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 11.2 — Speech LLMs: three audio grafts onto an LLM]{.tag}

1.  **Audio-in**: the speech encoder (Whisper, HuBERT) is projected into the LLM's space by an adapter (SALMONN, SpeechGPT, and all multimodal assistants 2025+) — the model *listens* (implicit transcription, paralinguistics: emotion, speaker) and answers in text; it is the "audio-in" family of ch. 8 of the LLMs module (M2), same machinery as vision;
2.  **Audio-out**: the LLM generates *acoustic tokens* (VALL-E: AR over EnCodec with a voice prompt; AudioLM units at the output); the cloning of ch. 9 becomes a skill of the language model;
3.  **Audio-in-out (speech-to-speech)**: Moshi (ch. 10): the text is the *inner monologue* guiding the audio tokens in both directions — the LLM *is* the pipeline.

    SpeechT5 (2022) had laid down the first unified text/speech architecture (T5 encoder-decoder + shared codebook); 2024-2026 generalize: one model, all the module's tasks (ASR, TTS, speech translation, editing, voice to voice).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 11.3 — Multilingualism: 7,000 languages, 100 covered]{.tag} The bottleneck of low-resource languages: labeling is expensive, writing is sometimes lacking.

**MMS** (Meta, 2023 — "Scaling Speech Technology to 1000+ Languages"): a single wav2vec 2 model covers 1,107 languages in ASR *and* TTS (4,017 in language identification), learned on public religious readings (the paradox: the Bible is the most translated text in the world) — a jump by a factor of 10-40 in coverage.

**Common Voice** (Mozilla): open crowd-sourcing (including French — regional accents: lab 1 draws from it).

The specificities of French return (ch. 4, ex. 4.3): number normalization (the date sub-test: "en 1996"), acronyms, loanwords.

For the engineer: zero-shot (Whisper/MMS) first, light adaptation next (LoRA on the encoder: a trainable low-rank update of the frozen weights, [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch4) ch. 4; versioned adapters in production: ML Ops module M2 ch. 7), targeted data last; and measure *per language* — a multilingual "average" WER masks local collapses.
:::

::: note
[Conclusion of the module — the fusion of the three worlds]{.tag} Signal (M1), language (LLMs M2), conversation (this module): speech is no longer an interface *in front of* language, it becomes one of its dialects — discrete tokens like any others, generatable, guidable, controllable.

The control of the *Control in Generative AI* module (M2, ch. 2: the taxonomy) now applies word for word: hard constraints = SSML and prosody grammars; guidance = style tokens and cloning by prompt; watermarking = voice provenance (ch. 9); evaluation = WER/MOS/latency and trade-off curves.

Wherever you set foot in 2026 — research or product — the final question is the same: *what must be controlled, and at what price?*
:::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **★ Lab: Whisper transcription and WER (the module's ASR lab).** With `transformers`:

    a.  load `openai/whisper-tiny` as an ASR pipeline, transcribe two French excerpts from Common Voice (one read, one spontaneous);
    b.  implement the WER (word-level Levenshtein alignment: $S + D + I$ against the reference);
    c.  compare tiny/small;
    d.  pre-filter with Silero VAD (cut the silences) and measure the effect on the hallucinations of (a);
    e.  redo on English to situate French.

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): tiny is 2-3× faster but clearly more fragile; the spontaneous French WER is 1.5-3× read English; the VAD massively reduces the hallucinated loops on silences (Whisper "invents" text without energy — prop. 4.2 experienced); beware of normalizations (capitalization, punctuation: normalize before aligning, otherwise the WER is artifactual). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
2.  **★ Lab: TTS with transformers (the synthesis lab).**

    a.  synthesize a French text with a public TTS model (SpeechT5; French MMS-TTS);
    b.  measure the RTF (computation time / audio duration) and the first-sample latency;
    c.  try three trap sentences: "1 234 567 €", "le SARS-CoV-2", "à Saint-Étienne, il est 19 h58" — record the normalization failures;
    d.  inject a different speaker embedding and compare.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: RTF $<$ 1 on GPU, on the order of 1-3 on CPU; the first-sound latency is dominated by the length of the first Mel *chunk*; numbers and acronyms fail reproducibly — discuss neural vs rule-based front-end (def. 8.3); the embedding shifts the timbre but not the regional accent: perfect zero-shot cloning does not exist with a single vector (ch. 9: one needs the sequential prompt, VALL-E style). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
3.  **★ CTC by hand.** Take up example 2.2 ($T = 4$, $y = \texttt{ab}$) with, for $t = 1..4$,
    $$p_t(\epsilon) = 0.5, \qquad p_t(a) = 0.3, \qquad p_t(b) = 0.2 .$$
    Compute the 15 products, sum them, check that the sum equals the $\alpha_4(5) + \alpha_4(4)$ obtained by the recursions of Theorem 2.3 (fill in the $\alpha$ table row by row).

    ::: proof
    Guidance: the $\alpha$ table has 4 rows $\times$ 5 columns (with structural zeros — one cannot reach $\ell_4$ before $t=2$). Its last row and the result are
    $$(0.0625, 0.0816, 0.171, 0.0864, 0.06), \qquad p(y \mid x) = 0.0864 + 0.06 = 0.1464,$$
    the sum of the 15 products.

    Six paths tie as the most probable (two blanks, one $a$, one $b$: $0.5^2 \times 0.3 \times 0.2 = 0.015$ each), whereas the frame-by-frame argmax is $\epsilon\epsilon\epsilon\epsilon$, which collapses to the empty string — the best path is not the best labelling.

    Check that the bound $T \geq |y|$ (here 2) is necessary and explain the jump condition $\mathbf 1\{\ell_s \neq \ell_{s-2}\}$ on a counter-example "aa". [∎]{.qed}
    :::
4.  **★★ CTC in code, gradient verified.** Implement $\alpha$, $\beta$ (thm. 2.3) in NumPy for a mini-vocabulary; compute $\partial \mathcal L/\partial p_t(k)$ by the closed formula; check against automatic differentiation (autograd/PyTorch of the sum of paths) to within $\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: the convention ($\beta$ with or without the $p_t$ factor) is the classic error — the autograd check detects it immediately; measured complexity $\mathcal O(T S)$ versus enumeration (15 paths here; enumeration explodes beyond $T \approx 15$); conclude on the differentiation *of the full model's objective* (softmax + recursions) — this is exactly what PyTorch does, vectorized. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
5.  **★★ Latency budget of a voice assistant.** A pipeline: VAD (30 ms window) $\to$ chunking ASR (640 ms chunk, 160 ms lookahead) $\to$ LLM (time-to-first-token 250 ms) $\to$ TTS (first Mel chunk 120 ms + vocoder 20 ms).

    a.  compute the first-sound latency of the response (component-by-component detail);
    b.  identify the two dominant terms and propose three reductions;
    c.  compare with Moshi's full-duplex (\~200 ms theoretical): what does it remove?

    ::: proof
    Guidance:

    a.  sum the delays after the user's last word:

        -   VAD 30 ms;
        -   endpointing — absent from the list but unavoidable — a silence threshold of 300-500 ms;
        -   ASR chunking: the last word is transcribed only once its 640 ms chunk and the 160 ms lookahead have been heard, i.e. on average half a chunk plus the lookahead ($320 + 160 = 480$ ms) and up to 800 ms;
        -   LLM 250 ms;
        -   TTS $120 + 20 = 140$ ms.

        Total, of which endpointing and chunking make about two thirds:
        $$\approx 30 + 400 + 480 + 250 + 140 \approx 1.3 \text{ s on average (up to } \approx 1.7 \text{ s)};$$

    b.  reduce the threshold by end-of-turn prediction (prop. 10.2), ASR with a smaller chunk, speculative LLM (referral to LLMs M2 ch. 6);

    c.  Moshi removes VAD/endpointing (continuous stream prediction), ASR/TTS (native audio tokens) and the LLM queue: what remains is network time + one model step. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
6.  **★★ Audio watermarking: ROC under attack (bonus).** Synthesize 20 sentences (lab 2); mark half of them with a public audio watermark (e.g. AudioSeal); plot the detector's ROC (true positive / false positive) on: clean audio, mp3 re-encoding at 64 kbps, light noise addition; conclude on the end-to-end provenance channel (ch. 9).

    ::: proof
    Guidance: the clean curve is nearly perfect (AUC $>$ 0.99); mp3 degrades moderately (the watermark survives usual compressions — it is designed for that); strong additive noise attacks harder; relate to the robustness budget (Control module ch. 10): marking strength $\uparrow$ = imperceptibility $\downarrow$ — the same triple trade-off as in text. [∎]{.qed}
    :::

### A classical assessment {#projects-exam}

Since no mode is published, this design follows the balanced default of these notes: a written exam on the eight sessions, two graded labs and one project with a live demonstration.

| Component | Weight | Format | Covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Written exam | 50 % | 2 h, no documents, one handwritten A4 sheet | ch. 0–11 |
| Lab reports | 20 % | Ex. 1 (Whisper and WER) and Ex. 2 (TTS), 10 % each; notebook and 2-page note each | sessions 3 and 5–6 |
| Project | 30 % | one card of the [list below](#projects-list), or the ASR → LLM → TTS loop with the ROC of Ex. 6; report and 10-minute oral with a live demonstration | sessions 1–8 |

**Resit.** A 2 h written exam on ch. 0–11 replaces the exam component; the lab and project marks are kept, and a missing project can be handed in once more and graded on the same grid.

**Sample questions.** Five questions of 4 points each, a 20-point paper of 2 h.

**Q1 (4 pts) — CTC by hand.** Alphabet $\{\epsilon, a\}$, target $y = \texttt{a}$, three frames, and at every frame $p_t(\epsilon) = 0.6$, $p_t(a) = 0.4$. (a) List the paths that collapse to $y$. (b) Fill the forward table of theorem 2.3, then give $p(y \mid x)$ and the loss. (c) What does greedy decoding output, and what does this show?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Writing `-` for the blank, six paths: `--a`, `-a-`, `a--`, `-aa`, `aa-`, `aaa`; the path `a-a` is excluded, since it collapses to `aa` (1 pt).
- (b) With the extended label $(\epsilon, a, \epsilon)$, the rows are (0.6, 0.4, 0), then (0.36, 0.40, 0.24), then (0.216, 0.304, 0.384). Hence $p(y \mid x) = 0.304 + 0.384 = 0.688$, which matches the sum of the six products, and the loss is $-\ln 0.688 \approx 0.374$ (2 pts).
- (c) The frame-wise argmax is the blank three times, which collapses to the empty string, of probability $0.6^3 = 0.216$ only: the best path is not the best labelling, and a beam search that merges prefixes (proposition 2.4) recovers $\texttt{a}$ (1 pt). Common error: allowing the jump of two positions onto the final blank.
:::

**Q2 (4 pts) — Word error rate.** Reference "le chat dort sur le canapé", hypothesis "le chat sort sur canapé bleu". (a) Compute the WER with an alignment. (b) Can a WER exceed 100 %? Give an example. (c) Name one normalization pitfall and its effect on the score.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) The word-level edit distance is 3: one substitution (dort → sort), one deletion (the second "le") and one insertion ("bleu"); an alignment with three substitutions is also optimal. With 6 reference words, WER = 3/6 = 50 % (2 pts).
- (b) Yes, because insertions are not bounded by the reference length: "oui" recognized as "oui oui merci beaucoup" gives 3/1 = 300 % (1 pt).
- (c) Case, punctuation and number formats must be normalized on both sides before aligning: otherwise "Canapé." against "canapé", or "19 h" against "dix-neuf heures", count as errors and the WER measures formatting, not recognition (1 pt).
:::

**Q3 (4 pts) — Latency budget.** A cascade assistant uses a 500 ms silence threshold for endpointing, a chunked encoder with 32-frame chunks, an 8-frame lookahead and a 10 ms frame step, an LLM with a 250 ms time to first token, and a TTS whose first chunk and vocoder take 150 ms.

(a) Give the algorithmic latency of the recognizer (Definition 5.1) and the worst-case delay between the user's last word and the first sound. (b) Which two terms dominate? Propose two changes that bring the total to 800 ms or less, with numbers. (c) What does a full-duplex model remove?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) $(32 + 8) \times 10 = 400$ ms (1 pt); worst case $500 + 400 + 250 + 150 = 1{,}300$ ms (1 pt).
- (b) Endpointing and chunking dominate. For instance, an end-of-turn predictor allowing a 200 ms threshold (proposition 10.2) and 16-frame chunks with a 4-frame lookahead (200 ms) give $200 + 200 + 250 + 150 = 800$ ms; any justified combination is accepted (1 pt).
- (c) The VAD and the endpointing decision, the separate recognizer and synthesizer, and the queue between them: both audio streams are predicted continuously, with about 200 ms of theoretical latency (theorem 10.3) (1 pt). Common error: forgetting the lookahead or the endpointing threshold.
:::

**Q4 (4 pts) — Flows and flow matching.** (a) A one-dimensional flow maps $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ to $x = 1 + 2z$: compute $\log p(x)$ at $x = 3$ by the change of variables.

(b) For conditional flow matching with $x_0 = (0, 1)$, $x_1 = (2, -1)$ and $t = 0.25$, give $x_t$ and the regression target. (c) Why does a normalizing flow have an exact likelihood when a VAE does not, and what does flow matching trade it for?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) $z = (3 - 1)/2 = 1$, so (1.5 pts)
  $$
  \log p(3) = \log \mathcal{N}(1;\, 0, 1) - \log 2 = -0.5 - 0.919 - 0.693 \approx -2.112 .
  $$
- (b) $x_t = 0.75\, x_0 + 0.25\, x_1 = (0.5,\ 0.5)$ and the target velocity is $x_1 - x_0 = (2, -2)$ (1 pt).
- (c) A flow is a bijection with a tractable Jacobian, so the change of variables gives the density exactly, whereas a VAE only bounds it by the ELBO (VITS is a VAE and uses its flow only to make the prior density exact). Flow matching is not trained by likelihood but by regression on velocities, which needs no simulation during training and allows sampling in few steps; its likelihood would require integrating the divergence of the field along the trajectory (1.5 pts). Common error: forgetting the $-\log 2$ Jacobian term.
:::

**Q5 (4 pts) — Interpretation.** (a) "CTC marginalizes alignments, Whisper generates them": explain, and give one typical failure of each. (b) Why is TTS watermarking easier than text watermarking? Name one transformation that still degrades an audio mark.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) CTC sums over all monotone alignments with frames independent given the input (theorem 2.3): it has no internal language model, hence spelling errors on homophones without an external LM. Whisper's attention decoder emits the text, and the timestamps as tokens, autoregressively: the alignment is learned and the decoder is a language model, but it can hallucinate or loop on silences (proposition 4.2) (2 pts).
- (b) Audio is continuous with a huge channel capacity: a low-energy, key-dependent signal hidden under the psychoacoustic threshold is detected by a correlation test without audible cost, whereas each mark on discrete, low-entropy text tokens costs quality and a paraphrase removes it (theorems 9.2–9.3) (1 pt). Transformations: low-bitrate MP3 re-encoding, resampling, additive noise or reverberation, re-voicing by voice conversion (1 pt).
:::

### Projects {#projects-list}

Every project uses public data, a laptop CPU or one free Colab T4 GPU, and only what this module and its prerequisites (Signal Processing, Large Language Models, one Deep Learning course) teach. Levels ★/★★/★★★ are those of the exercises, and the effort stays at most 20 h per student, as for a 24 h / 2 ECTS course.

**Grading grid used by every project of this page** (a project card may replace one row).

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Question and success metric stated before the experiments | 10 % |
| Correct use of the course results (cited by number) | 25 % |
| Protocol: leakage-free split, baselines, at least 3 seeds, intervals | 25 % |
| Results and analysis: error analysis, limits, one responsible-AI remark | 20 % |
| Reproducibility: repository, README, pinned environment, one command | 10 % |
| Communication: report (≤ 6 pages solo, ≤ 10 group) or 10-minute oral | 10 % |

Group projects: a contribution statement and an oral with individual questions; the individual grade is the group grade times a factor in [0.8, 1.2].

#### P1 · ★★ · solo · French ASR under telephone conditions {#proj-1}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Measure the WER of Whisper small on French read speech, clean and degraded to telephone conditions, with and without VAD and text normalization: report the WER with bootstrap intervals and the number of hallucinated insertions on 50 clips padded with 5 s of silence, against the clean, normalized baseline. |
| Data | [FLEURS fr_fr](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/fleurs) — CC BY 4.0 — 3,193 / 289 / 676 read utterances (train / validation / test); loading: `load_dataset("google/fleurs", "fr_fr", split="test")`. Degradation, fully specified: resample to 8 kHz, band-pass 300–3400 Hz, add babble made of 6 other test utterances at 10 dB SNR (seed 0). Model [Whisper small](https://huggingface.co/openai/whisper-small) (Apache 2.0), [Silero VAD](https://github.com/snakers4/silero-vad) (MIT) |
| Chapters | [ch. 0](#ch0) (sampling, telephone band, Definition 0.1), [ch. 4](#ch4) (proposition 4.2, example 4.3), [ch. 5](#ch5) (the VAD note); extends Ex. 1 ([exercises](#ex)) |
| Deliverables | notebook and 4-page report |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 15 h per student · free Colab T4, longest run ≤ 30 min (676 clips under four conditions) |
| Objectives served | O6 (communication, public services), O7 (deployment conditions), O5 (audio modality) |
| Responsible AI | FLEURS speakers recorded under a CC BY 4.0 release: report the WER per speaker gender (field `gender`) and attempt no speaker identification. |
| Going further | Per-accent WER on Common Voice French (CC0, free Mozilla Data Collective account). |

#### P2 · ★★ · solo · A CTC recognizer from scratch {#proj-2}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Train a small BiLSTM-CTC character recognizer with a hand-written forward-backward checked against autograd: report the gradient error (target ≤ $10^{-6}$) and the test-clean WER of beam search with prefix merging (beam 8) against greedy decoding. |
| Data | [LibriSpeech](https://www.openslr.org/12) — CC BY 4.0 — train-clean-100 (100 h, 251 speakers), of which the first 25 speakers by ID (≈ 10 h) are used, and test-clean (2,620 utterances, 5.4 h); loading: `torchaudio.datasets.LIBRISPEECH("data", url="train-clean-100", download=True)` |
| Chapters | [ch. 0](#ch0) (log-Mel features), [ch. 2](#ch2) (Definition 2.1, theorem 2.3, proposition 2.4), [ch. 3](#ch3); extends Ex. 3 and Ex. 4 |
| Deliverables | notebook and 4-page report |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 20 h per student · free Colab T4, longest run ≤ 2 h (≈ 5 M parameters, 30 epochs on 10 h) |
| Objectives served | O1 (derivation and gradients), O7 (implementation) |
| Responsible AI | LibriSpeech readers are mostly North American volunteers: report the WER per speaker sex (`SPEAKERS.TXT`) and state the accent limitation of the model. |
| Going further | A Conformer block (proposition 3.2), or shallow fusion with an n-gram language model. |

| Field | Content |
|---|---|

### End-of-year projects {#projects-capstone}

Two Year-2 capstones of the transverse project use this module: the bilingual voice assistant of [C4](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c4) (ch. 4, 5, 7, 9, 10: streaming recognition, synthesis, watermarked and disclosed voice, endpointing) and the optional voice channel of the public-agency assistant of [C8](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c8) (ch. 4, 5, 7, 11: WER per accent group as an equal-access measure). The module brings the latency budget and the per-group WER that both capstones report.
